_note: Environmental observations per analog site and finding (protected areas, fragile features, wildlife, season windows, climate hazards, impact rules, pressure on the site). Planning information only: never changes a score. Proposed by the analysis team; boxes are approximate. Revised 2026-11-15: misattributed and duplicated notes removed, Peru block added, verification_status set per note (verificado = source opened and confirmed on 2026-11-15; oficial_sin_reabrir = official source not re-opened; pendiente = unconfirmed or weak source, do not act on it; secundario = context from secondary/news source). Still planning information only: never changes a score.

environmental_notes.text: Surface soil microbial communities in the hyperarid core are adapted to near-total dryness; after rare rains (2015, 2017) 75-87% of pre-rain species became undetectable. Wetting or disturbing soils during sampling can destroy the communities being studied.

Summer (Dec-Mar) 'altiplanic winter' storms reactivate dry rivers in northern Chile and cause floods and debris flows (e.g., Rio Loa, Calama); Chile lacks a flood early-warning system for these events.

areas.name: Desierto de Atacama, María Elena Sur

environmental_notes.text: Surface soil microbial communities in the hyperarid core are adapted to near-total dryness; after rare rains (2015, 2017) 75-87% of pre-rain species became undetectable. Wetting or disturbing soils during sampling can destroy the communities being studied.
Maria Elena Sur is drier than Yungay (mean air RH 17.3%, soil RH about 14% at 1 m) and still hosts viable bacteria in its soil profile, making undisturbed profiles scientifically valuable.

Summer (Dec-Mar) 'altiplanic winter' storms reactivate dry rivers in northern Chile and cause floods and debris flows (e.g., Rio Loa, Calama); Chile lacks a flood early-warning system for these events.

Under the National Lithium Strategy, Salar Grande is part of ENAMI's state lithium project group (with Infieles, Isla and Aguilar), and a network covering at least 30% of salares is to be protected. Whether Salar de Pajonales is protected or under concession was not confirmed.

Halite nodules host endolithic and epilithic consortia from all three domains of life plus viruses, kept alive by moisture from frequent coastal fog; breaking or removing nodules destroys these habitats.
Laguna Colorada is described as the most important flamingo breeding site in the world and the main breeding ground of the threatened James's flamingo; breeding success varies strongly between years.
Laguna Colorada was listed as a Ramsar site in 1990, later enlarged to the Los Lipez Ramsar site (about 1.43 million ha), half inside Eduardo Avaroa Andean Fauna National Reserve.
The Licancabur summit crater lake (about 5,900 m) hosts diverse microbes and cyanobacterial mats on the lake bottom; it is ice-covered roughly April-September.
UV radiation at about 6,000 m is the main stressor even for lake microbes; field teams face extreme UV and severe altitude.

Licancabur sits on the Chile-Bolivia border: the summit and crater lake are reached from the Bolivian side inside the Eduardo Avaroa Andean Fauna National Reserve (see Ramsar 489). The Chilean flank faces San Pedro de Atacama; whether it falls inside any sector of Reserva Nacional Los Flamencos (CONAF, created by D.S. 50/1990 of the Ministry of Agriculture, seven sectors, about 73,987 ha) was not confirmed. Crossing the border on foot requires both countries' controls.

Whether Salar de Pajonales is inside the protected salar network of Chile's National Lithium Strategy or under a mining concession was not confirmed; check the CONAF and SERNAGEOMIN registries before planning fieldwork.

Gypsum domes, crusts and living stromatolites host specialized cyanobacteria and archaea; about 10% of non-polygon gypsum habitats are colonized by endoliths, so trampling or driving on gypsum crusts can destroy rare microhabitats.
Gypsum here also preserves fossil stromatolites and diatom frustules (biosignature archive); the authors flag it as a priority Mars astrobiology target, which argues for minimal-impact sampling.
Laguna Negra and Laguna Tres Quebradas are listed in the Ramsar site 'Lagunas Altoandinas y Puneñas de Catamarca' (designated 2 February 2009, about 1.23 million ha, Argentina's largest).
In 2024 a Catamarca court ordered lithium activity at Salar del Hombre Muerto halted after a complaint by an Indigenous community leader, which shows active disputes over Puna water and land.
Puna lagoons host living stromatolites and microbial mats forming large mounds on lagoon floors; high Andean wetlands also hold extremophile microbial communities.
Local tourism providers allege that a lithium operation near Fiambala is drying mountain lagoons (Laguna Verde reportedly down up to 5 m); Laguna Negra itself is not confirmed as affected.
Argentine NGO FARN argues salt flats are wetlands and highlights water use by lithium extraction across the Puna.

Hyperarid soils (e.g., 'Mar de Cuarzo') hold less organic matter than Yungay and very low, patchy microbial populations, with patches differing even a few metres apart; contamination and disturbance can bias life-detection tests.
Previously unstudied endolithic and epilithic lichens were reported here, among the first reports of these organisms in this desert.
Four years of monitoring (2004-2008) documented extreme temperature, moisture and radiation conditions; specific hazard thresholds not confirmed here.

No national protected area is known at Pampas de La Joya, but the cell must be checked against the SERNANP map, including buffer zones. Under Ley 26834 (Protected Natural Areas Law, Articles 18 and 20) any protected area's Master Plan is binding for every activity inside it, as the 2025 Tambopata resolution restates.

Any work that disturbs the ground in Peru needs the Certificado de Inexistencia de Restos Arqueologicos en Superficie (CIRAS) from the Ministerio de Cultura, regulated by Decreto Supremo 011-2022-MC (Reglamento de Intervenciones Arqueologicas); Decreto Legislativo 1680 (2024) added the Diagnostico Arqueologico de Superficie as an alternative. Drilling, trenching or heavy-vehicle tests on the pampa fall under this requirement.

The pampas around La Joya hold registered pre-Hispanic sites: the Gross Munsa geoglyph archaeological landscape (Santa Isabel de Siguas, 4.05 ha, UTM 18S 810903 E / 8192288 N) was declared Patrimonio Cultural de la Nacion by Resolucion Viceministerial 000220-2022-VMPCIC/MC, whose Article 4 requires prior Ministry of Culture approval for any nearby works, and which cites Ley 28296 Article 6.1 (pre-Hispanic sites are intangible State property). The La Caldera petroglyph field (La Joya district) is the second largest in Arequipa after Toro Muerto.

In 2019 the Majes Siguas II irrigation consortium was refused an archaeological clearance after Wari geoglyphs were found on the Siguas pampas, which shows that clearance can be denied on these plains; plan rover tracks and sampling points only after the Ministry of Culture review.

Collecting soil microbes, lichens or any wild flora or fauna outside protected areas needs SERFOR's research authorization (Ley 29763, Forestry and Wildlife Law; guidelines RDE 060-2016-SERFOR/DE), and taking samples out of Peru needs SERFOR's scientific export permit. The astrobiology work that made La Joya an analog (soil organics, endolithic lichens) falls under this rule.

The Peruvian Air Force's La Joya Air Base (Grupo Aereo N.4, fighter aviation) lies on the same pampa; expect restricted airspace for drones and military-use land nearby. The restricted-zone boundaries and the DGAC drone rules for the area were not confirmed; ask the FAP and DGAC before flying anything.
Altiplano pre-rainy season (Sep-Nov) rainfall has declined over 40 years and models predict a drier Dec-Feb rainy season; seasonal flooding creates the shallow pools flamingos use.

Lithium projects on the salar are criticized by local scientists for lacking environmental impact assessments required by Bolivia's 1992 Environmental Law; communities push back against foreign-backed projects.

Wastewater analysis at the lithium operation found elevated arsenic, a possible threat to flamingos via brine shrimp; brine pumping may also lower groundwater and cause subsidence, as seen at Salar de Atacama.
Bolivian salt flats support flamingo populations that depend on seasonal brine pools.

Standard NPS permit conditions ban mechanized equipment in designated, proposed or potential wilderness unless the superintendent authorizes it in specific conditions. NPS history sources put designated wilderness at about 91% of the park (other NPS-linked pages say about 93%).
Driving off designated roads is illegal in the park, and in most places the wilderness boundary starts 50 feet from designated roads. Bicycles are not allowed off roads, on trails or in wilderness.

Summer temperatures can reach 130-134 F; heat kills 1-3 people a year, and the park discourages low-elevation hiking after 10 a.m. in summer. Helicopters may be unable to fly in extreme heat, so field work belongs in the cool season.
Flash floods: remnants of Hurricane Hilary (20 Aug 2023) gave the park's wettest day on record, closing all roads and the park for about two months.
The park maintains official flash flood guidance; canyons and washes are the danger zones.
Field work (Haughton-Mars Project) runs in the short Arctic summer, with a core team on the island through summer only.
Polar bears occur on the island and are a lethal hazard to field teams.
Continuous permafrost with a thin summer active layer; summer temperatures about -5 to +5 C with sleet and snow, and thaw produces mud that vehicles can rut.
The endemic wekiu bug lives only on summit cinder cones above about 3,500 m, mainly near crater rims; cinder disturbance affects its habitat.

Altitude sickness: spend at least 30 minutes at the Visitor Information Station (about 2,800 m) before going higher; pregnant women, people in poor health and children under 13 should not go above it.
Winter snow and ice cause injuries and road closures; rangers urge 4WD and caution.
Driving motor vehicles off-road is forbidden in Iceland. The exception is glaciers and frozen or snow-covered ground outside urban areas with no apparent risk of damage.
Highland road F88 to Askja has opened between 14 June and 1 July in recent years and has large river fords; access is roughly late June to September.
A 21 July 2014 rockslide into the caldera caused a tsunami in Oskjuvatn reaching about 400 m inland; IMO expects further rockslides.
Ground uplift since 2021 (over 70 cm) indicates magma accumulation; Civil Protection uncertainty level in force, bathing in Viti discouraged and prolonged stays not recommended.
Activities need prior environmental assessment and authorization by the national authority of the organizing country. Entering an Antarctic Specially Protected Area needs a special permit.

The Dry Valleys are Antarctic Specially Managed Area No. 2 (Measure 18, 2015); following its management plan is a legal obligation under US and New Zealand law, and it holds five ASPAs (123, 131, 138, 154, 172).
ASMA No. 2: the largest ice-free region in Antarctica, with coordinated management.
Code of conduct asks visitors to prevent cross-contamination between sites.
Human DNA contamination measured in soils at camps.
Cross-country vehicle driving and motorcycles or quads off paved roads or tracks are banned in the Parajes Naturales. After research, the ministry inspects the site for damage.

Decree 558/2004 declared the Río Tinto Protected Landscape (Paisaje Protegido), whose aims include conserving the geomorphology created by mining. The use regime in its Article 4 was not read, so specific sampling rules are not confirmed.
The river corridor is also a Special Area of Conservation (ZEC ES6150021, Corredor Ecológico del río Tinto), with a management plan approved 8 May 2015.

Acidic river (mean pH 2.3, 92 km) with high metal loads and unexpectedly high acidophile diversity (iron-oxidizing Leptospirillum, Acidithiobacillus); sampling should avoid disturbing microbial biofilms.
Waters carry Fe, Cu, Zn and As at high concentrations, a contact hazard for people and equipment.

areas.name: San Francisco Volcanic Field y Cinder Lake

environmental_notes.text: Cinder Lake lies inside the Coconino NF Cinder Hills OHV Area (about 13,500 acres), where riding is on designated routes; the Apollo crater field was blasted in 1967.
Cinder cones erode easily and scars heal slowly: the nearby Sunset Crater summit trail was closed in 1973 and its scars remain decades later.
Heavy OHV use has required restoration work in the Cinder Hills OHV Area, which can alter the historic Apollo crater field surface.
Privately owned (Barringer Crater Company) National Natural Landmark; rim access is via guided walks only. Rules on sampling or collecting are not confirmed and must be asked of the operator.
MDRS crews operate roughly late autumn to spring; summer heat ends the field season and the hot months are used for maintenance.
Colorado Plateau biological soil crusts (cyanobacteria, lichens, mosses) stabilize soil; damage can take 50-250 years to recover, so stay on trails, slickrock or washes.
The Barstow Field Office reports a court-ordered closure of desert tortoise critical habitat to OHV use in the West Mojave planning area. Whether it affects Dumont Dunes is not confirmed.
The Mojave fringe-toed lizard, a dune specialist, is listed as 'sensitive' by BLM and has been petitioned for protection.

A federal court order closed desert tortoise and Lane Mountain milk-vetch critical habitat routes in the West Mojave to OHV use from 24 March 2026; whether Dumont Dunes lies in that habitat is not confirmed.
Dumont Dunes is a 7,620-acre BLM OHV recreation area, so vehicle driving on dunes is a permitted use; check BLM maps for closed zones.
The monument includes designated wilderness, where the standard NPS permit conditions bar mechanized equipment unless specifically authorized.
A free cave permit is required to enter lava tubes, as a measure against white-nose syndrome; the fungus was confirmed in Idaho in 2022 but not detected at the park.
Visitors must observe cave closures, avoid caves with hibernating bats, and use different clothing and gear if they have visited other caves (decontamination).
Cave access operates under interim guidance until a new Cave Management Plan is completed.
The basin is Kameshtashtan National Historic Site, a cultural landscape of profound meaning to the Mushuau Innu within their hunting territory; fieldwork requires Innu engagement.
Nickel-copper smelting left about 17,000 ha of barren land and 64,000 ha of stunted forest; metals remain bioavailable in acidic soils.
A regreening program since 1978 (lime, fertilizer, seeding, tree planting) has reclaimed roughly half the landscape; disturbing limed, revegetated soils can undo restoration.
Cuatrociénegas was decreed a Flora and Fauna Protection Area in 1994, is administered by CONANP and is a Ramsar wetland.
One of the rare places with living stromatolites and microbial mats, a relict bacterial niche in a desert oasis.
Canals, deep wells and alfalfa irrigation have drained wetlands and interrupted aquifer recharge; dry stromatolites are now common along the main road.
Federal operations have closed illegal water wells in the valley.
Area de Proteccion de Flora y Fauna (1994) managed by CONANP; swimming in pools has long been restricted, with only Las Playitas reopened under strict controls.
El Pinacate y Gran Desierto de Altar is a CONANP-managed federal biosphere reserve and was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2013.
UNESCO World Heritage Site (2013) and Biosphere Reserve covering 714,566 ha of volcanic shields, craters, lava flows and dunes.
The US border wall disrupts wildlife movement, including the endangered Sonoran pronghorn; the World Heritage Committee has urged action.
Conservation groups have pushed for listing the site as World Heritage in Danger due to border-wall impacts.
Cross-country vehicle driving and motorcycles or quads off paved roads or tracks are banned in the Parajes Naturales. After research, the ministry inspects the site for damage.
Paraje Natural (Law 2/1989) and Natura 2000 site (ZEC and ZEPA bird protection area).
Ramblas are dry most of the year but fill during 3-4 days of torrential rain annually, often producing flash floods.
Birds nest in rambla banks and walls; endemic plants include Euzomodendron bourgaeanum and endangered Limonium insigne.
Collecting, destroying or damaging minerals or plants is generally prohibited. Researchers must restore the site afterwards and report results to the president (Arts. 48-49).

Motor vehicles may use only marked tracks, with a 40 km/h limit and no groups of five or more vehicles (Arts. 15-16). Special transit permits on restricted tracks and temporary camps may be granted for research (Art. 47), and recreational drones are banned (Art. 40).
The Comunidad has closed areas to all visitors during bird nesting season, which in 2024 coincided with military air exercises at the range.
Access to some zones (e.g., Rallon, Pisquerra, La Balsa, Zapata) is closed from mid-February to end of August for bird breeding; exact zones vary by source, check the park centre.
UNESCO Biosphere Reserve with raptors (griffon vulture, golden eagle) and steppe birds (great bustard, Dupont's lark).
An Air Force firing range (about 2,244 ha) operates inside the park since 1951; a June 2026 proposal to end it was rejected in Congress.
Because the ecosystems are fragile, access to the reserve zone is allowed only for scientific or management purposes.
UNESCO World Heritage Site (2007) recognized for volcanic features and endemic flora.
The Teide violet grows only above about 3,000 m on Teide and is described as the park's most fragile species; off-trail walking risks it.
Visitor crowding causes trail erosion and disturbance to endemic flora; since late 2024 trails on Teide and Pico Viejo slopes need a free permit (not fully confirmed).
The endemic blind squat lobster Munidopsis polymorpha lives in the anchialine pool of Jameos del Agua, where the La Corona tube meets the sea.
Its population dropped after construction and opening of Jameos del Agua for tourism.
The Bavarian Environment Agency (LfU) states that 'geotope' is not a legal protection category. Where protection is needed, sites are designated under nature conservation law or as monuments.
UNESCO Global Geopark Ries lists about 150 geotopes including the Altenburg suevite quarry, where coesite and stishovite proved the impact origin.
The Alte Burg suevite quarry is reported as inside a protected area; individual outcrop protection status is not confirmed.
Whether specific anorthosite outcrops lie in a protected area (for example Lofotodden National Park), and what Norwegian motor traffic rules mean for rover tests, is not confirmed.
One of the finest anorthosite exposures on Earth, used for ESA PANGAEA lunar geology training; no specific environmental restriction found (not confirmed).
Fossil digging is a major livelihood (about 70% of Erfoud residents depend on it by local estimates); over-excavation and weak controls damage paleontological heritage.
Meteorite hunting is intense and largely unregulated ('finders keepers').
Colorful hydrothermal salt and iron-rich deposits are fragile and at risk from unprotected tourism; visible damage to delicate structures has been reported.
Gaet'ale spring nearby emits deadly gas (almost certainly CO2) evidenced by dead birds; hydrothermal areas warrant extreme caution.
Access is via approved agencies only, with security and Afar community participation as conditions.
Sua Pan is among the world's top ten breeding sites for lesser and greater flamingos; breeding depends on rainy-season flooding.
The pan floods (about 30 cm) from Nata River inflow during the rains, may stay dry in poor years, and rapid drying can force chicks to walk over 50 km.
A soda ash plant on the NE edge of Sua Pan has lowered the water table; veterinary fence collisions kill adult flamingos.
Vehicle tracks on central Namib gravel plains reduce lichen cover by up to 80% and ruts can persist for decades.
Gobabeb's restoration unit works on rehabilitation of vehicle track scars; staying on existing tracks is the standard rule.
Namib Sand Sea World Heritage Site (2013): fauna depends on fog, with high endemism; water extraction and mineral exploration are emerging threats.
Dalangtan playa salts (Mg sulfates, chlorides, perchlorates) and yardangs covering about 20,000 km2 resemble Martian features.
Tso Kar Wetland Complex became a Ramsar site in December 2020.
Key breeding site for black-necked crane; the basin is undisturbed June-October, matching the crane breeding season.
Grazing and unregulated tourism (garbage) are main threats.
Ramsar site (2020), Wildlife Sanctuary and National Geo-heritage Monument.
Sewage from the town and rising water levels threaten the lake; causes debated.
The lake turned pink in 2020 due to haloarchaea, indicating sensitive saline microbial communities.
Collecting or exporting meteorites without permits violates Omani law; authorities combat smuggling.
Over 3,600 meteorites have been recovered from Dhofar and Al Wusta, and illicit collecting depletes the fields.
Ramon Crater is an INPA-managed nature reserve of about 1,100 km2 and an International Dark Sky Park. Part of its land lies within the Israel Nuclear Research Center site.
Nubian ibex are commonly seen in the reserve.
Stay on designated tracks to protect fragile desert crusts.
Negev wadis flood very suddenly; check forecasts (not confirmed for the crater specifically).

BirdLife lists Armash fish farm as an Important Bird Area and Key Biodiversity Area of 4,639 ha, mostly privately owned, and reports illegal and legal shooting of waterbirds there. The site has been proposed for Ramsar status but is not confirmed as designated.
Armash fishponds IBA: more than 230 bird species recorded, with breeding of White-headed Duck and other threatened species; a major flyway stopover.
Emerald Site since 2016 and potential Ramsar site.
Waterbirds are shot due to conflict with fish-farming.

Five Pilbara early-life sites have been declared State Geoheritage Reserves, and permission is needed to visit or sample in them. The oldest microbial structures in the historic North Pole mining area are within Buick Reserve.
3.48 Ga stromatolites in the North Pole Chert Member are irreplaceable evidence of early life.
Pilbara summers (Dec-Feb) regularly exceed 40 C with thunderstorms and cyclones; park closures occur.

Off-road motor traffic on bare, unfrozen ground is allowed only on designated routes or with a Governor permit (Svalbard Environmental Protection Act s. 80). Aircraft landings outside approved strips also need an exemption (s. 83).

Bockfjorden lies in Nordvest-Spitsbergen National Park, which specifically protects its thermal springs, carbonate deposits and volcanic remains. A 2020 amendment (s. 5b) bans travel within a mapped zone at Trollkjeldene.
Anyone travelling outside settlements must carry suitable means to scare off polar bears, and the Governor recommends carrying a firearm. Renting a rifle generally needs a police lending permit.
The world's northernmost terrestrial hot springs; plants and mosses found nowhere else in Svalbard grow in about 1,000 m2 around them.
Inside Nordvest-Spitsbergen National Park; a permanent traffic ban applies around the Trollkjeldene springs.
Anyone outside settlements must carry means of scaring polar bears, and the Governor recommends a firearm.
Continuous permafrost and dry polar climate; the only road in Greenland reaches Point 660 and Russell Glacier.
Rivers swell with meltwater as summer progresses and glacial outburst floods (jokulhlaups) have become more frequent locally.
Field campaigns are typically a few weeks each summer.

areas.name: Corn Belt, Iowa (control negativo de cultivo intensivo)
Amazonía sur, Reserva Nacional Tambopata, Madre de Dios (control negativo)

environmental_notes.text: SERNANP approved the Reserva Nacional Tambopata Master Plan for 2025-2030, the area's top planning document, which sets use zones. The zone-by-zone rules were not reviewed.

areas.name: Cuenca de Qaidam este, playa de Qarhan (China)

environmental_notes.text: Qarhan liquid potash output and grade are declining, and alkaline solution mining can cause environmental harm.

areas.name: Tierras bajas del Kolyma, Duvanny Yar (Rusia)

environmental_notes.text: Yedoma stratotype, ice-rich and highly vulnerable to thermokarst and erosion.
Thaw streams release CO2 and turbidity in the Kolyma rises by about 20% downstream.

areas.name: Macizo del Tibesti, volcan Emi Koussi (Chad)

environmental_notes.text: More than half of Chad's mined area is in Tibesti; no survey in over a decade due to insecurity.

Zorkul Lake Ramsar Site No. 1086 (3,800 ha, centred 37.38 N, 73.33 E, designated 2001) lies about 30 km east of the point, inside Zorkul Nature Reserve, which is also a BirdLife IBA/KBA. Whether the point itself falls inside the reserve boundary is not confirmed.

Tajik National Park (Mountains of the Pamirs) is a World Heritage property covering much of the eastern Pamir; IUCN treats Zorkul as a separate neighbouring reserve linked by a wildlife corridor project. Overlap of the point with the World Heritage boundary is not confirmed.

Snow leopard and Marco Polo argali are the flagship mammals; argali lambing is in the second half of May and first half of June and the rut is around December-January, so spring calving and winter rut periods should be avoided near herds.

Bar-headed goose breeds on islands in Zorkul Lake (60-125 pairs, 2000-2006), the species for which the area was first protected in 1972; avoid the lake shores and islands in the summer breeding season.
Very high, cold and arid plateau: the eastern Pamirs record winter temperatures below -50 C, and nearby Murghob sits at about 3,600 m, so altitude sickness and cold limit fieldwork outside summer.

IUCN notes off-road driving on 4WD tracks as a (low) threat to fragile alpine desert, waste disposal and littering as a problem, and use of teresken shrub as fuel as a concern if visitor numbers rise; vehicles should stay on existing tracks and all waste and fuel should be brought in and out.

Munkhkhairkhan National Park (about 5,061 km2, Khovd and Bayan-Olgii, snow leopard, argali and Siberian ibex habitat) is centred about 50 km north of the point; Bulgan Gol Nature Reserve (beaver, sable, stone marten) lies on the border with China to the south-west. Overlap of the point with either is not confirmed.
Permafrost underlies about 29% of Mongolia, continuous in high-altitude areas and degrading under warming; ground disturbance in high Altai terrain may accelerate thaw.
Off-road vehicle tracks are a major land-degradation driver in Mongolia; in central Mongolia revegetation of abandoned tracks takes roughly 10-15 years, so rover tests should reuse existing tracks.
Khovd is among the western provinces repeatedly rated high or very high dzud (severe winter) risk; winter lows in western Mongolia reached -47 C in January 2024.
Snow can persist in the Altai into June in some years, so the practical window is summer; a station-based field-window source was not found (not confirmed).

Mongolia's Law on Specially Protected Areas (15 Nov 1994, consolidated text) allows in the virginal (core) zone only research and observation-based study that does not disturb the natural state (Article 9), so any test inside a park core zone would be excluded.
No protected area, Ramsar site or IBA/KBA was found at the Kokcha point; Afghanistan has only 15 protected areas in WDPA and the search could not list their boundaries, so absence is not confirmed.

Markhor and Siberian ibex were documented in northern Badakhshan (Darwaz, Shahr-e Buzurg) in 2011, with the Amu Darya strip proposed as a priority area that also matters for snow leopard; these sites are north of the point and presence at the point is not confirmed.
Uncontrolled hunting of wild and rare birds has increased substantially in Badakhshan, threatening several species.
Badakhshan is classed as a high avalanche-risk province and roads are closed every winter by snow and avalanches, isolating districts.
Spring snowmelt and heavy rain cause flash floods and avalanches (for example February 2023), and frequent earthquakes in north-east Afghanistan trigger landslides.
Winter road closures imply a summer-autumn window, but no dedicated source on a safe field season was found (not confirmed).

areas.name: Tian Shan oriental, vertiente de Toksun

environmental_notes.text: Xinjiang Tianshan World Heritage (2013) has four components including Bogda (Fukang/Urumqi side); Bogda is also a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve since 1990. No source places the Toksun slope inside a component, so overlap is not confirmed.

Urumqi Glacier No. 1 (about 60 km west, a long-term monitored glacier) has retreated throughout 1962-2006, its terminus averaging about 4.4 m per year and its two branches separating in 1993; glaciers and monitoring installations in this range should not be disturbed.
Toksun county regularly issues strong-wind warnings for the 'thirty-mile wind zone' with gusts of force 10-12 and sand and dust, which can damage equipment and stop drone flights.
The Turpan Depression, where Toksun lies, often exceeds 40 C in summer and receives under 20 mm of precipitation per year.
Tian Shan glacial lakes grew 148% in number between 1990 and 2023, raising outburst-flood risk, and China warned of extreme summer floods in Xinjiang in June 2026 linked to heat and glacier melt.

Otgontenger Strictly Protected Area (declared 1992, about 955 km2) surrounds the Khangai's highest peak about 40 km east of the point; it is also a state-sanctioned sacred mountain. Overlap of the point with the SPA is not confirmed.
Otgontenger Mountain is a Key Biodiversity Area listing argali, Siberian ibex and snow leopard (Endangered).
Otgontenger holds the only permanent glacier in the Khangai range, and locals report steady recession of snow levels.
In the Khangai forest-steppe, near-surface discontinuous permafrost is limited to large forest stands on north-facing slopes, so these patches are sensitive to disturbance.
Zavkhan is one of the western provinces repeatedly rated high or very high dzud risk, with extreme winter cold; fieldwork is realistically a summer activity (dedicated window source not found).
No federal or regional protected area was confirmed at the point; regional resource reserves exist in the Verkhoyansk and Abyy districts (for example Tuostakh), but overlap is not confirmed.

The Yana-Indigirka lowland is part of the ice-rich Yedoma domain, where drained thermokarst basins cover up to 80-100% of low terrain; the IRYP v2 map should be checked at the exact cell. Vehicle traffic on ice-rich ground can trigger thermokarst.
Permafrost prevails across the Selennyakh Range itself.

The Critically Endangered Siberian crane breeds on about 82,000 km2 of tundra between the Yana and Kolyma rivers (densest at Kytalyk, farther north); laying is late May-early June and departure mid-August to early October. Use of the 68 N interfluve is not confirmed.
The CMS Siberian crane programme lists human disturbance from oil exploration and development in Yakutia as a significant threat, relevant to any motorised field campaign in breeding habitat.
The upper Yana-Indigirka basins hold the Northern Hemisphere pole of cold; Verkhoyansk averages -44.7 C in January and +16.5 C in July, so work is effectively limited to the short summer.

areas.name: Meseta de Putorana (sectores sureste y norte)

environmental_notes.text: The site is UNESCO World Heritage (2010), and within the core reserve no land or resource use is allowed other than scientific research and monitoring. Access is by helicopter or water, with no road.
Putorana Plateau World Heritage (2010) coincides with the Putoransky State Nature Reserve; whether the 68.0 N, 97.5 E cell lies inside the reserve or its buffer zone is not confirmed.
One of the largest wild reindeer migration routes crosses the property, and the plateau hosts the endemic Putorana snow sheep (Russian Red Book) and is a key staging area for Arctic migratory birds.
IUCN reports that climate change is causing permafrost thaw and vegetation change in the property.
Snow cover lasts about eight months and melts fully only in mid-June, and lakes carry about 2 m of ice for about six months, so the field window is roughly late June to early September.
Sulphur dioxide from Norilsk smelters on the plateau's western edge is a major pollution source; the reserve buffer is 80-100 km from production sites.
Northern Ellesmere is inside Quttinirpaaq National Park; offshore, the Milne Ice Shelf lies in the Tuvaijuittuq Marine Protected Area (2019), which does not extend onto land.

The Milne Ice Shelf lost 43% of its area in 2020 and its epishelf lake has since drained; Ward Hunt Ice Shelf also fractured in 2011-2012. These collapsing ice shelves are both fragile and hazardous to work on.

Parks Canada requires packing out all garbage and toilet paper, human waste 100 m from water and camps, no collection of plants, rocks or fossils, no disturbance of rocks at possible archaeological features, a permit for aircraft landings, and no recreational drones; research needs a permit.

Park monitoring records muskox herds near Lake Hazen and small Peary caribou herds (7 animals in two sightings); Parks Canada guidelines prohibit disturbing wildlife and require avoiding nesting, calving and denning areas.
24-hour daylight runs May-August and the recommended visiting period is late May to mid-August, but winter conditions can occur at any time.

No protected area was confirmed at Meidob; Wadi Howar National Park (proclaimed 2001, about 100,000 km2, UNESCO Tentative List) lies to the north, but its boundaries were not found, so overlap is not confirmed.
The field has about 700 vents and some 30 maars; Malha crater (about 150 m deep) holds the only remaining crater lake, a rare permanent desert water body.
Wadis radiating from the field carry water during flash floods.

For North Darfur (El Fasher data, about 250 km south-east), rain peaks July-August and highs reach about 41 C in May; the cooler dry months (about November-February) look most workable, but no Meidob-specific source was found.
Armed conflict in the Sahara-Sahel has been linked to steep declines of dorcas gazelle (Vulnerable); current Darfur or Meidob wildlife data were not found (not confirmed).
Abbasabad Wildlife Refuge (about 3,000 km2, desert and steppe east of Naein) is close to the point; exact boundary overlap is not confirmed.

Abbasabad is one of the remaining habitats of the Critically Endangered Asiatic cheetah, with caracal, wild sheep and goitered gazelle; a cheetah was camera-trapped there after about 14 years without records.
Five of Iran's eight wild felid species have been recorded in the Abbasabad reserve.
Desert climate on the edge of the Dasht-e Kavir, with summer maxima around 41 C and winter minima around -9 C; blowing dust occurs.
No environmental rules specific to vehicles, drones or sampling at this site were found (not confirmed).

No protected area, IBA or Ramsar site was found at the point; the nearest found is the fenced Mahazat as-Sayd Protected Area (oryx and houbara reintroduction) about 170 km north-east of Taif, which does not appear to overlap. Absence is not confirmed.
Harrat Rahat has about 1,000 small volcanoes and a historical lava flow (1256 AD, near Medina far to the north); fresh flow surfaces are geoheritage.

North-west Arabian harrats host prehistoric stone structures (mustatils, kites, pendants, stone circles), and 5 of 10 sites proposed for UNESCO's 'Prehistoric stone structures' tentative listing are harrats; a Rahat-specific inventory at the point was not found (not confirmed).

Saudi Arabia's Executive Regulation for Vegetation Cover (NCVC) requires a permit for specific activities on vegetation-cover land, including camping (fine 500 SR per camp), cutting trees or shrubs and grazing; it does not require a licence for land use in general. Confirm whether a rover test counts as camping or as a licensed activity.
Desert climate with 60-100 mm rain, mostly December-February, and occasional severe flash floods in the Medina region (for example August 2024).

Harrat Khaybar holds dense prehistoric stone structures: mustatils (about 7,000 years old, among the oldest monumental structures known), kites of shapes unique to Khaybar, pendants and funerary avenues, surveyed by the AAKSAU Khaybar project since 2019. Rover driving or sampling could damage them.

The Khaybar aerial archaeology project produced some of the first radiometric dates for 'pendant' (tailed cairn) monuments in Saudi Arabia, showing these structures are a dated, scientifically important resource on the harrat.
No WDPA site, IBA or Ramsar site was found on western Harrat Khaybar; the harrat is under intensive land-use and tourism development (not confirmed as protected).

Saudi vegetation-cover rules require a licence for activities on vegetation-cover lands; in nearby AlUla the Royal Commission fines vehicle activity that damages vegetation (500 then 1,000 SAR). Whether the AlUla rule applies at Khaybar is not confirmed.
Khaybar is named in regional flash-flood and storm events (for example November 2015), and the Medina region gets most of its 60-100 mm annual rain in winter.

environmental_notes.text: Naybandan Wildlife Refuge spans about 31.8-33.4 N and 55.5-57.5 E (about 14,000-15,000 km2), so the point sits on or near its eastern edge; overlap is possible but not confirmed.
Naybandan is described as the most important Asiatic cheetah habitat, with animals moving between Naybandan and Ravar refuges; cheetahs prey on wild goat, wild sheep and gazelle there.
ThinkHazard rates Tabas extreme heat as High and earthquake as Medium.
June-August highs average about 39-40 C with almost no rain, so summer field tests are heat-limited; cooler months are preferable (dedicated field-window source not found).
South Khorasan was among 25 provinces hit by flash floods from December 2025.
